solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Old pair of keys — somehow he cut two more the same — snap!

indicators.note: 'somehow' says the letters arrive by some unstated route, so their order is not fixed

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
F is a musical key, so a pair of them is two Fs
these five letters rearranged
another two of the same key, F and F

explanation.surface: Someone recounts an old key-cutting job: two keys duplicated twice over, with a triumphant 'snap!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snap!' looks like the card-game cry for matching pairs, but it is the adjective, as in a snap decision.
explanation.definitionFit: A snap judgement is made instantly without preparation, just like an impromptu off-the-cuff remark.

clue.text: Prospect of deliveries dismissing Surrey's openers?

indicators.note: openers are the ones who go in first, so each word contributes only its leading letter

parts.note: the initial letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A cricket question: what are the chances of the bowling getting rid of Surrey's opening batsmen?
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture invites thinking of balls and wickets, but 'openers' simply takes the first letters of the words in front of it. Surrey is an English county cricket team.
explanation.definitionFit: Odds are the likelihood or chances of something happening, which is what a prospect means.

clue.text: Following rule leads to breach

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
a law is a rule

explanation.surface: Sticking rigidly to the rulebook can end up causing a breach.
explanation.definitionFit: A breach is a gap or crack, and a flaw is likewise a crack or fault in something.

clue.text: If moving, they'll receive a tug, right as stern comes adrift

definitions.text: If moving, they'll receive a tug

indicators.note: something that comes adrift drifts loose from its moorings, so the letters break free of their order

parts.note: the twelve letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A nautical scene: a drifting ship whose stern has broken loose is taken in tow by a tug.
explanation.walkthrough: The tug and stern suggest a boat, but the definition is about emotion: a moving story is said to tug at the heartstrings.
explanation.definitionFit: Something emotionally moving is idiomatically said to tug at your heartstrings, the seat of deep feelings.

clue.text: Caught with reduced thrust, getting stuck

indicators.note: something reduced has been cut down, here losing its final letter

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a lunge is a forward thrust, as in fencing

explanation.surface: A fencer, caught out with a weakened lunge, ends up stuck.
explanation.definitionFit: To have clung to something is to have stuck fast to it, past tense of cling.

clue.text: Brother, in secret, beginning to fix me up — within reason

indicators.note: the beginning of the following word means only its first letter is wanted

parts.note: first letter of fix

indicators.note: within says one piece sits inside another

parts.note: taken as written, as the outer shell

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the word from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, then turned upwards

explanation.surface: A secretive brother asks someone to set him up, within reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brother, in secret' defines a member of the famously secretive fraternity, whose members call each other brother; 'up' reverses because this is a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Freemasons are a secretive fraternal society whose members address one another as brothers.

clue.text: English flower found around Lake Placid

indicators.note: being found around something means wrapping round it on both sides

parts.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Cam is the English river through Cambridge
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A traveller notices an English bloom growing by a still lake, with a nod to Lake Placid in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lake Placid' reads as the place name, but the words split: Lake gives a letter and Placid is the definition. 'Flower' is the crossword river.
explanation.definitionFit: Placid and calm are synonyms describing something still, untroubled and peaceful.

clue.text: Entirely normal to get hernia? Not entirely

indicators.note: the phrase is not used in full, so only a stretch from inside it is wanted

parts.note: a run of consecutive letters spanning these words

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether getting a hernia is perfectly normal, then hedges.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Entirely' is the definition and 'Not entirely' signals the hidden answer, a neat echo.
explanation.definitionFit: Altogether means wholly or completely, a direct synonym of entirely.

clue.text: Scrapping of loco met with cry for transport alternative

indicators.note: scrapping breaks something up for parts, so the letters are taken apart and rebuilt

parts.note: the ten letters of loco, met and cry, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The scrapping of a railway engine is met with protest from those wanting other transport.
explanation.walkthrough: Loco is short for locomotive, a railway engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorbike is one means of getting about instead of the train, so it is a transport alternative.

clue.text: One that's excessively emotional, Democrat with hit piece about head of agency

indicators.note: the two words before go about, that is surround, the following piece

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics
to ram is to hit hard

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of agency
the queen is a chess piece

explanation.surface: An overwrought Democrat is linked to a hatchet-job article about an agency boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit piece' reads as a smear article, but the words split: hit and piece each give a part, flanking A.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama queen is an idiom for a person who reacts to everything with exaggerated emotion.

clue.text: Begin — right away, immediately

indicators.note: sending something away removes it from the word

parts.note: to start is to begin
R is the abbreviation for right; it is the letter taken out

explanation.surface: An order to get going straight away, without delay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' looks like the idiom for at once, but here right is a letter being sent away; 'immediately' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stat is medical jargon from Latin statim, used in hospital dramas to mean at once.

clue.text: Couple relaxed around noon, becoming bored

indicators.note: around says the first word wraps itself about the next piece

parts.note: to couple is to join or unite
N is the abbreviation for noon
having relaxed is having rested

explanation.surface: A couple lazing about at midday grow bored of each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone uninterested feels no curiosity or engagement, which is how a bored person feels.

clue.text: Theatre worker turned a handle hidden in floor

indicators.note: being hidden in something means sitting inside it

parts.note: to floor someone is to stagger or astound them

indicators.note: turned round means the letters run the other way

parts.note: a handle is slang for a name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A theatre hand turns a handle concealed in the stage floor, perhaps working a trapdoor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor' looks like the stage boards, but it is a verb: to floor is to astonish.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage manager runs the backstage side of a theatrical production, so is a theatre worker.

clue.text: Not moving investment — it's up a couple of pounds

parts.note: stock is an investment in shares

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written, then turned upwards
L is the abbreviation for pound (from libra), so two of them

explanation.surface: A dormant investment has gone up by just a couple of pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' seems to describe the investment rising, but it turns the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock-still means completely motionless, so it describes something not moving.

clue.text: Knackered, overwhelmed by allotment, drank last of prosecco

indicators.note: being overwhelmed by something means being engulfed inside it

parts.note: an allotment is a share, a cut; it forms the outer shell
lapped means drank with the tongue, as a cat does

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: last letter of prosecco

explanation.surface: An exhausted gardener at their allotment knocks back the end of the prosecco.
explanation.walkthrough: The allotment invites a garden plot, but here it means a share. Knackered is British slang for worn out or broken down.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapped-out is British slang for worn out and no longer working, the same sense as knackered.

clue.text: Everyone's into alcohol-free drinks — lies!

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: TT stands for teetotal, abstaining from alcohol; it forms the outer shell
everyone is all
ales are drinks of beer

explanation.surface: Everyone is drinking alcohol-free beverages, or so they claim, which is a lie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alcohol-free drinks' reads as one phrase, but it splits: alcohol-free is the teetotal abbreviation and drinks are the beers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall tales are exaggerated, unbelievable stories, which is to say lies.

clue.text: Fight Korea's top brass after officer goes to the north

indicators.note: heading north in a down clue means travelling upwards, reading bottom to top

parts.note: COL is the abbreviation for colonel

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Korea
horns are brass instruments

explanation.surface: A military clash: Korean top brass fight after an officer heads into the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top brass' reads as senior officers, but top takes a letter and brass is musical instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Stags lock horns when butting heads, so the idiom means to fight or clash.

clue.text: Sharp refusal to accept empty threat

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it in, so it goes inside

parts.note: nay is a refusal, an old word for no

indicators.note: emptying a word removes its insides, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: outer letters of threat

explanation.surface: A curt refusal to be cowed by a hollow threat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp' seems to describe the refusal, but it is the definition in its sense of smartly dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: Natty and sharp are both informal words for smart and stylish in dress.

clue.text: Vehicle keeps parking by island — this one?

definitions.note: points back to the island just named: the answer is that very island

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A car is parked beside an island, and the clue asks whether the car is named after it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This one?' is the definition: the answer is itself an island, Capri in the Bay of Naples, and also the name of a Ford car, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Capri is an island off Naples, and the Ford Capri sports coupé was a vehicle named after it.

clue.text: Fish that's gone bad in angler's basket

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside another
something gone bad has spoiled, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

parts.note: these four letters rearranged
a creel is a wicker basket for carrying caught fish

explanation.surface: An angler finds a fish has gone off in their basket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone bad' reads as one rotten phrase, but bad tells you to rearrange gone.
explanation.definitionFit: The conger eel is a large marine eel, and an eel is a type of fish.

clue.text: One breaking rocks in prison having gone across border with heroin

indicators.note: in says the following pieces sit inside the prison word

parts.note: the slammer is slang for prison; it forms the outer shell
an edge is a border
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A convict breaking rocks on a chain gang, jailed for smuggling heroin over the border.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture of a convict breaking rocks is the definition itself: the tool, not the prisoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A sledgehammer is a heavy long-handled hammer used for smashing stone, hence a rock breaker.

clue.text: Contend with flash in picture

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a flash
to vie is to contend or compete

explanation.surface: Competing with a camera flash when someone is taking a photo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contend with' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'with' just joins the two pieces, which go in the reverse of clue order. MO is British slang for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture is an informal word for a film, as in going to the pictures.

clue.text: Squashed by slate, one's hurt

indicators.note: being squashed by something means being pressed inside it

parts.note: to slate and to pan both mean to criticise harshly
one is the Roman numeral I; the 's stands for is, joining to the definition

explanation.surface: Someone crushed under a slab of slate is injured.
explanation.walkthrough: Slate looks like the roofing stone, but it is the verb meaning to criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurt as a noun means pain or suffering, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Tip of little finger goes black

indicators.note: the tip of something is its very end, here the front letter of the finger word
the tip goes, meaning that front letter is dropped and the rest kept

parts.note: pinky is an informal name for the little finger

explanation.surface: The end of a little finger turns black, perhaps from frostbite or a trapped nail.
explanation.walkthrough: The tip that goes is the first letter of the finger word; the remainder is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ink is typically black, so inky describes something dark or black.

clue.text: Press club

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to press clothes smooth with a heated appliance
second meaning: a type of golf club with an angled metal head

explanation.walkthrough: Together the words suggest a journalists' club, but they are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for smoothing creases from clothes and a noun for a golf club.

clue.text: Into scrap, very crafty in retirement — easy money made on this

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it

parts.note: a grain is a scrap, as in a grain of truth; it forms the outer shell
V is the abbreviation for very

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: arty means crafty in the sense of arts and crafts; it is turned round

explanation.surface: A wily pensioner gets into the scrap-metal trade, a nice little earner.
explanation.walkthrough: Crafty looks like cunning, but it means arty, as in arts and crafts.
explanation.definitionFit: A gravy train is an idiom for a job or scheme that pays well for little effort, so easy money is made on it.

clue.text: Ultimately, casual pick-up that has strings attached

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun: a thing that has strings

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: last letter of casual
a ute (utility vehicle) is the Australian word for a pick-up truck

explanation.surface: A casual hook-up that turns out to come with strings attached after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strings attached' sounds like emotional obligations in a romance, but it is literal: the instrument is strung.
explanation.definitionFit: A lute is a plucked string instrument, so it literally has strings attached.

clue.text: Authority finally defeated in French city after case is scrapped

indicators.note: in says the letter is placed inside the city name
after places the city-and-letter group second, behind the jumbled word that follows it in the clue

parts.note: these four letters rearranged

indicators.note: a scrapped item is broken up, so its letters are reassembled differently
finally points to the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of defeated
Nancy is a city in north-eastern France; it is the outer shell

explanation.surface: An authority figure, finally beaten in a French city once the case against them is dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case is scrapped' reads as a dropped prosecution, but it means the word case is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascendancy is a position of dominance or control, which is authority.
